newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Defiant Israel says building starts next week.
newsitem.headline: Defiant Israel says building starts next week.

text.p: Defying warnings of violence and a torrent of world criticism, Israel intends to break ground next week on a disputed Jewish settlement in Arab East Jerusalem, a cabinet minister said.

The settlement plan is at the heart of what former prime minister and peacemaker Shimon Peres called on Wednesday the "biggest crisis in Israel's ties with the PLO and the Arab world" since its landmark 1993 peace deal with the Palestinians.

Jordan's King Hussein warned there was a "very strong chance of violence" if Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu pushed ahead with plans to build 6,500 homes for Jews on the wooded hilltop called Jabal Abu Ghneim by Palestinians and Har Homa by Israel.

Internal Security Minister Avigdor Kahalani told army radio he discussed the plan with Netanyahu on the prime minister's return Wednesday night from a visit to Russia: "We agreed between us that next week the work will begin on Har Homa."
Kahalani's statement coincided with a U.N. debate in which the PLO urged the General Assembly to denounce the plan and other Israeli policies it said violated the peace process.
A resolution calling on Israel to rescind the plan was expected to be adopted by an overwhelming majority late on Thursday.
The resolution is almost the same as one vetoed by the United States in the Security Council last Friday. Arab states, frustrated by the veto, took the issue to the 185-member General Assembly.
In Gaza, Palestinian President Yasser Arafat voiced hope a meeting of U.S., European and Arab envoys on Saturday would rescue Middle East peace from the deepening crisis.

Israeli-PLO relations -- which warmed briefly after the Jewish state pulled its troops from most of the West Bank town of Hebron in January -- have plunged into turmoil over recent Israeli steps, notably the settlement plan.
Nobel peace laureate Peres told Israel Television Channel One that if the sides escalated the crisis "we will destroy the chance for peace in the Middle East."
Asked by the radio if bulldozers would arrive at the site next week, Kahalani said, referring to a large Caterpillar tractor: "The order has gone out to a D-9 to begin to move."
Faisal Husseini, head of Jerusalem affairs for the Palestinian Authority, has said Palestinians would bar bulldozers with their bodies if Israel tried to begin work.
Israel sees Jerusalem as its undivided capital while the PLO views East Jerusalem, captured by the Jewish state in the 1967 Middle East war, as the capital of a future Palestinian state.

The United States, Israel's closest ally, tightened the noose of international pressure around the Jewish state on Wednesday by saying it would send Edward Abington, the consul general in Jerusalem, to the Gaza meeting.

In an apparent effort to calm Israeli fears, Washington later said the Saturday forum called by Arafat was an important chance for him to air concerns but was no substitute for direct talks with the Jewish state.
Wrapping up a visit to Russia, Netanyahu was combative when asked about mounting world criticism of his policies.
He told a Moscow news conference he was "fed up" with charges Israel was violating peace deals with the Palestinians.
Deputy Housing Minister Meir Porush, leaving Israel a potential escape, said the government would take "as long as the matter requires" to surmount court challenges to building at the site.

He noted that investigators of a high-level government scandal had promised results in 10 days and were taking two months. "Here, too, this (waiting) could continue, but not with the intent of refraining from building Har Homa," he told Israel Radio. Hawks called this evidence of caving in to Arab pressure.

Palestinians accuse Netanyahu of trying to circumvent them as his peace partners and of violating Israeli-PLO peace accords by planning to build the settlement, which they say compromises talks due to decide the fate of East Jerusalem by 1999.

Palestinian wrath was further stoked by Israel's decisions to hand over less than a third of the West Bank land the PLO expected in a withdrawal planned for this month, and by warnings Israel would close four Palestinian offices in East Jerusalem.
